title: Ethiopian Shiro Powder
community: All of Ethiopia — the pantry staple
author: Mama Tigist
desc: Ethiopian Homemade Shiro Powder — roasted chickpeas, dried onion, garlic powder, berbere, and ground spices ground together into the pre-seasoned flour used for Shiro Wat. Making shiro powder at home produces a dramatically superior result to commercial versions.
longDesc: Homemade shiro powder is a revelation — where commercial shiro is often bland and one-dimensional, home-made shiro from freshly roasted chickpeas with a custom berbere blend produces a Shiro Wat of extraordinary depth.
ingredients: 2 cups dried chickpeas (or yellow split peas)
steps: Dry roast chickpeas in a heavy pan over medium heat for 18—20 minutes, stirring constantly, until deeply golden and nutty-smelling.
Grind roasted chickpeas to a fine powder.
Add berbere, garlic powder, onion powder, turmeric, ginger, cardamom, and salt.
chefTips: Roast chickpeas very thoroughly — light roasting produces a starchy, flat shiro.
The grinding must be fine — coarse shiro produces a grainy Shiro Wat.
Home-made shiro powder makes dramatically better Shiro Wat than commercial powder.
Yellow split peas can substitute for chickpeas — slightly different flavour.
commonMistakes: Light roasting — insufficient depth of flavour.
cookingScience: See ETH102 for shiro cooking science. Home-made shiro retains the volatile aromatic compounds from freshly roasted chickpeas — these begin dissipating immediately after grinding. Commercial shiro, ground weeks earlier, has lost most of these volatile aromatics, which is why home-made is dramatically superior.
sustainabilityTips: Chickpeas — nitrogen-fixing, drought-resistant, and the most sustainable legume available.
servedWith: Stored as a pantry staple for fasting periods
storage: Airtight jar — 6 months. Freeze for longer.
healthBenefits: The berbere in the shiro powder provides significant antioxidants.
culturalNote: Home-made shiro powder is the mark of the committed Ethiopian cook — the person who takes the time to roast and grind their own chickpeas produces Shiro Wat at a quality level that commercial shiro cannot match. Ethiopian grandmothers make their own shiro powder the same way their grandmothers did.
